procedural_history.originating_court: Trial court in Special (ACB) Case No.10 of 1992
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of the High Court of Gujarat dated 16.04.2015 in Criminal Appeal Nos. 477 and 478 of 2000.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Gujarat reversed the verdict of conviction passed by the trial court, thereby acquitting the respondents under Section 7 and Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, set aside the High Court's judgment, and affirmed the conviction of the accused Nos. 1 and 2 under Section 7 and Section 13(1)(d) of the Act. The sentence of imprisonment under Section 13(1)(d) of the Act imposed upon each of the accused was reduced from two years to one year.

decision.appeal_result: The impugned judgment of the High Court dated 16.04.2015 in Criminal Appeal Nos.477-78 of 2000 is set aside and these appeals are allowed.
decision.conviction_status: The conviction of the accused Nos.1 and 2 under Section 7 and Section 13(1)(d) of the Act is affirmed.
decision.sentence_status: The sentence of imprisonment under Section 13(1)(d) of the Act imposed upon each of the accused is reduced from two years to one year.
directions: The respondents/ accused Nos.1 and 2 shall surrender themselves to serve the remaining sentence within two weeks from today, failing which, they shall be taken into custody.

issue.issue_text: Whether the presumption raised under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act for an offence under Section 7 is a rebuttable presumption and whether the burden on the accused to rebut it is one of preponderance of probabilities.

law.fact_text: The Supreme Court affirmed that it is settled law that the presumption raised under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act for an offence under Section 7 is a rebuttable presumption.
law.relevant_text: it is settled law that the presumption raised under Section 20 of the Act is a rebuttable presumption

law.fact_text: The Court also affirmed that the burden placed on the accused to rebut this presumption is one of preponderance of probabilities.
law.relevant_text: the burden placed on the appellant for rebutting the presumption is one of preponderance of probabilities.

law.fact_text: This burden on the accused is not as high as the prosecution's burden to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
law.relevant_text: It is equally well settled that the burden of proof placed upon the accused person against whom the presumption is made under Section 20 of the Act is not akin to that of burden placed on the prosecution to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt…

law.fact_text: An accused can rebut the presumption either through the cross-examination of prosecution witnesses or by presenting their own reliable evidence.
law.relevant_text: The accuse charged with the offence could rebut it either through the cross-examination of the witnesses cited against him or by adducing reliable evidence.

application.fact_text: The Court noted that once the prosecution establishes that the accused was in possession of the bribe money, the presumption under Section 20 is triggered.
application.relevant_text: Since it is established that the accused was possessing the bribe money, it was for them to explain that how the bribe money has been received by them

application.fact_text: In this specific case, the Court found that the accused had failed to offer any satisfactory explanation to rebut the presumption.
application.relevant_text: The accused have not offered any explanation to rebut the presumption under Section 20 of the Act.

application.fact_text: Because the accused failed to rebut the presumption, the Court held that it must be presumed they accepted the bribe.
application.relevant_text: if he fails to offer any satisfactory explanation, it will be presumed that he has accepted the bribe.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that it is settled law that the presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act is rebuttable, and the burden on the accused to rebut it is based on a preponderance of probabilities, a standard lower than the prosecution's burden of proof.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the presumption raised under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act for an offence under Section 7 is a rebuttable presumption and whether the burden on the accused to rebut it is one of preponderance of probabilities.
appellant_arguments: It is settled law that the presumption under Section 20 of the Act is rebuttable, and the burden on the accused is one of preponderance of probabilities.
Since it was established that the accused were in possession of the bribe money, the burden was on them to provide a satisfactory explanation for how they received it.
The accused failed to offer any explanation to rebut the presumption that they accepted the bribe.
The evidence from the prosecution witnesses, establishing the demand for the bribe, was natural and credible.
The High Court erred in reversing the trial court's judgment, which was based on a proper appreciation of the evidence.
respondent_arguments: The arguments of the respondent are not detailed in the provided text.

cases.case_name: C.M. Girish Babu v. C.B.I. Cochin, High Court of Kerala
cases.principle: The presumption under Section 20 of the Act is rebuttable, and the burden on the accused to rebut it is one of preponderance of probabilities, not proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The accused can rebut the presumption through cross-examination or by adducing reliable evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The presumption raised under Section 20 of the Act is a rebuttable presumption, and the burden placed on the accused for rebutting it is one of preponderance of probabilities. If it is established that the accused was possessing bribe money, it is for them to explain how it was received, and if they fail to offer a satisfactory explanation, it will be presumed that they accepted the bribe.
obiter: The burden of proof placed upon the accused person against whom the presumption is made under Section 20 of the Act is not akin to that of the burden placed on the prosecution to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.
While appreciating evidence, the High Court should give proper weight to the views of the trial court as to the credibility of evidence.
When the findings recorded by the trial court are based upon appreciation of evidence, the High Court is not right in reversing the judgment of the trial court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the prosecution had successfully proven the demand and acceptance of illegal gratification through witness testimony and physical evidence, including the recovery of tainted currency notes and the presence of anthracene powder on both accused, which demonstrated they acted in tandem. This proof triggered the statutory presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The accused failed to offer any explanation to rebut this presumption, a burden which only required them to meet the standard of a preponderance of probabilities. Therefore, the High Court was not justified in reversing the trial court's conviction, which was based on a proper appreciation of the evidence.
legal_tests_applied: The presumption raised under Section 20 of the Act for an offence under Section 7 is a rebuttable presumption.

The burden of proof placed upon the accused person against whom the presumption is made under Section 20 of the Act is one of preponderance of probabilities, which is not akin to the burden placed on the prosecution to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.

Since it is established that the accused was possessing the bribe money, it was for them to explain how the bribe money has been received by them and if they fail to offer any satisfactory explanation, it will be presumed that they have accepted the bribe.
policy_considerations: While appreciating evidence, an appellate court (the High Court) should give proper weight to the views of the trial court as to the credibility of witnesses, and when the findings recorded by the trial court are based upon appreciation of evidence, the High Court is not right in reversing the judgment.
